Ok, I'm following you.

Not sure if this adds to the conversation, but I'll write down here what I know about atexit in glibc (which I presume is not the libc that nonstop uses)

1) an application calls atexit(fn) to register the function to be run when the application calls exit()
2) the glibc implementation of atexit() calls __cxa_atexit->internal_atexit, passing both the fn pointer to be registered and a pointer to a pointer to a list structure to add said function to
3) The list parameter passed to __cxa_atexit is named __exit_funcs.  Its a global structure with hidden visibility, and is part of the .data section of glibc, meaning its copy on write (i.e. whenever a process is forked that is linked to glibc, it gets its own copy of said pointer, effectively making it private to that process
4) on exit, the __exit_funcs list is traversed and all registered call back functions are executed
5) When complete, exit continues, the process is completed, libraries are unloaded, and all data pages (including the pages that contained the __exit_funcs pointer are reclaimed by the system.  If a new process is started, the glibc .data section page(s) that contain __exit_funcs are cow'ed again, and so we get an empty list for the new process.

Now thats glibc.  If the non-stop implementation is preserved accross forks, that would _very_ bad (unusable bad), as a process would have no idea what elements were on the list prior, which ones should be removed (if we could even tell that, which we cant), or when new handlers should be added.

I think we probably need to confirm your theory, and if its correct, we need to have a serious discussion about what to do about it.  Let me put together a debug branch for you.

so If I'm hearing you correctly, whats happening is that:
1) The application in question (here evp_extra_test), statically links to libcrypto.a.  as such when OPENSSL_init_crypto is called we use the statically linked RUN_ONCE variable to do the intial library setup, part of which is calling atexit(OPENSSL_cleanup)

2) The application then loads the legacy provider, which is dynamically linked to libcrypto.so, and  therefore loads a second copy of libcrypto into memory.  Some subsequent call path inside the provider calls OPENSSL_init_crypto (inside some text address for the dynamically loaded library), which then, because the .data section of said library is distinct from the statically linked version in the application. 
3) Because the memory space of libcrypto.so in (2) is distinct from the memory space of libcrypto.a in (1), the RUN_ONCE variable is still set to allow a single thread to process that init path, and when it does, it makes a second call to atexit(openssl_cleanup)
4) because atexit is defined in glibc, for which there is only a single in-memory instance, we now have 2 calls to OPENSSL_cleanup queued to be executed when the application exits.

If so, yuk.

We should be able to observe this with the debug code I added.  I've rebased it to the head of the 3.0.0 branch for you.

What I'm struggling with here though is, why should that matter?  I can see two possible outcomes of doing this:
1) We have two atexit calls to OPENSSL_cleanup pointing to two different instances of the function (one in the static library, one in the dymanic library
2) We have two atexit calls to OPENSSL_cleanup pointing to the same instance of the function (both in the static library or in the dynamic library)

If (1) is the case, then both calls should be ok to complete.  The first will tear down data in the static library, while the second will tear down data in the dynamic library.  Ugly, and definately something to avoid, but it _should_ work

If (2) is the case then the first call should complete without issue, and the second call should effectively be a no-op, as the stopped variable in that function will be set to 1, causing the function to return immediately.

But what we're seeing (It would seem), is some level of data corruption (based on the fact that the stack traces provided are in the atexit processing, rather than the library calls themselves), which suggests to me that there may be some amount of cross-data referencing occuring - i.e. the call path through OPENSSL_cleanup for one of the library instances is somehow referencing .data or heap in the other.

does nonstop do some level of symbol merging at load time?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: NonStop does not do symbol merging. However, `atexit()` is not in glibc on NonStop. It is in the CRE (Common Runtime Environment). In the CRE, there is one atexit list, but two entries of `OPENSSL_cleanup` and anything else registered twice. When the first DLL unloads, the instances of `OpenSSL_cleanup` get called but the list is not modified. When the program exits, the call is made to the instances are called again, but the memory for the procedure is no longer accessible, so SIGSEGV occurs. That's what was discovered last time (#17059).
